5.q: A water sample from a shower comes back positive for legionella. What is the appropriate response?
o: Throw the result away and re-sample only if someone later falls ill
Do nothing at all until the next scheduled annual review comes
Report it to the responsible person and follow the plan for disinfection
Increase the shower's flow rate to wash the bacteria away
5.w: A positive result is reported to the responsible person and the agreed remedial and disinfection actions are carried out to bring the system back under control.

n.0: Discarding a positive result hides a serious risk to health.
n.1: Waiting a year leaves a known contaminated aerosol source in use.
n.3: More flow spreads more contaminated aerosol rather than disinfecting the system.

5.q: Which practice would most undermine the control of a shower even if the quarterly cleaning is done on time?
o: Recording the exact cleaning date accurately in the site maintenance log each time
Descaling the shower head thoroughly before it is then properly disinfected
Rinsing the shower head with clean water once it has been fully disinfected
Leaving the shower full of stagnant water between cleans, never flushing it
5.w: Leaving the shower full of stagnant water and never flushing it between cleans lets Legionella multiply in the retained water regardless of the quarterly service, so regular flushing must accompany periodic cleaning.

n.0: Accurate recording supports control rather than undermining it.
n.1: Descaling before disinfecting is correct practice.
n.2: Rinsing after disinfection protects the user from residue.

5.q: What does the abbreviation ACOP stand for in relation to L8?
o: Approved Code of Practice
Annual Certificate of Practice
Approved Contractor Order Policy
Advisory Committee on Plumbing
5.w: L8 is the Approved Code of Practice, giving practical advice on complying with the law on legionella.

n.3: There is no such committee behind L8; ACOP is a defined legal term.
n.1: L8 is not a certificate; it is guidance with special legal status.
n.2: ACOP does not refer to a contractor order policy.

5.q: In terms of Legionella, why is a mixer tap or thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) area sometimes described as a higher-risk point for growth?
o: Because the water at that point is always stored well above 60°C
Because the mixing process removes all nutrients from the water
Because hot and cold blend to a warm temperature within the growth range
Because it only ever delivers cold water held well below 20°C
5.w: A TMV blends hot and cold to a comfortable warm temperature, which sits in the 20–45°C growth band right at the outlet and downstream fittings. This is why TMVs are fitted close to the outlet and maintained carefully.

n.0: The blended water is deliberately warm, not stored above 60°C.
n.1: Mixing does not remove nutrients; it produces a warm temperature ideal for growth.
n.3: The output is warm mixed water, not cold water below 20°C.

5.q: A legionella risk assessment should specifically consider people who are especially vulnerable. Which group is an example?
o: Delivery drivers who drop off at the gate and never go inside
Contractors who only ever work outside on the site grounds
People who merely park in the site car park and then leave
Elderly, sick or immunocompromised people who may be exposed
5.w: The assessment must consider those more susceptible to infection, such as the elderly, the sick and people with weakened immune systems.

n.0: People who do not enter the building are not exposed to its water aerosols.
n.1: Working outside on the grounds is not exposure to building water aerosols.
n.2: Using only the car park gives no exposure to the water system.

5.q: A visitor at a garden centre becomes unwell days after walking through a mist being sprayed over plant displays. Why is the misting system a plausible source to investigate?
o: Because the disease easily spreads from the other unwell visitors in the crowd on site
Because the visitors would surely have drunk the mist as they walked past it
Because mist can only ever be a risk if the water within it is ice cold
Because misting produces fine aerosols people can inhale, which can carry Legionella
5.w: Misting or humidification systems create fine breathable aerosols; if the water is contaminated, people passing through can inhale Legionella, so such systems are investigated.

n.0: The disease does not pass between people in a crowd.
n.1: Drinking is not the route; the concern is inhaling the aerosol.
n.2: Warm water favours growth; ice-cold water is not the risk condition.

5.q: Which of the following best describes 'so far as is reasonably practicable', the standard applied to many duties under HSWA 1974?
o: Only doing something once the HSE has specifically ordered it
An absolute duty that must always be met regardless of any other factor
Balancing the risk against the time, cost and effort to control it
Whatever the duty holder can still afford after all other spending
5.w: Reasonably practicable involves weighing the risk against the sacrifice (time, cost, effort) needed to reduce it; where the risk is significant relative to the effort, the control must be taken.

n.0: The duty exists independently of any HSE order.
n.1: It is not absolute; it explicitly allows a proportionate balance.
n.3: Affordability alone does not define the standard; risk is weighed.

5.q: A cold water storage tank is far larger than the building actually needs. Why is this a concern?
o: It uses far less energy overall, so there is really no downside at all
The stored water turns over slowly and can warm and stagnate
The stored water will end up far too cold for anyone to use
The tank will constantly overflow from being too large
5.w: An oversized tank holds more water than is drawn each day, so turnover is poor and the water can warm and stagnate.

n.0: There is a clear downside: poor turnover and stagnation risk.
n.2: Slow turnover tends to let cold water warm, not make it colder.
n.3: A float valve controls the level, so it does not overflow constantly.

5.q: What is biofilm, which can form inside shower hoses and heads?
o: A tough protective plastic coating fitted on the inside at the factory
A specialist cleaning product used to treat the outlets
A thin slimy layer of bacteria and matter clinging to the surface
A layer of ordinary hard limescale and nothing more than that
5.w: Biofilm is a thin slimy layer of bacteria and other matter that clings to internal surfaces and can shelter legionella.

n.0: It is not a factory coating; it is unwanted bacterial growth.
n.1: It is a problem to be removed, not a cleaning product.
n.3: Scale is different from biofilm, though the two often occur together.

5.q: Can Legionnaires' disease be fatal?
o: Yes, it can be fatal, especially in more vulnerable people
No, it only causes a mild and brief cold-like illness
No, nobody has ever died from the illness
Only if the person also happens to have a broken bone
5.w: Legionnaires' disease is potentially fatal, particularly in older or already unwell people.

n.1: It can be severe and cause pneumonia, not merely mild.
n.2: Deaths do occur, particularly among vulnerable groups.
n.3: A broken bone has nothing to do with the disease's severity.

5.q: An operative is asked to disinfect a cistern found heavily contaminated. What is the correct principle before returning it to service?
o: Clean out the debris and sludge first, then disinfect the now-clean surfaces
Leave the sediment in place so the disinfectant has something to work on
Disinfect it first and then clean out all the debris afterwards
Simply refill it with fresh mains water without cleaning or disinfecting
5.w: Physical cleaning to remove sludge and debris should precede disinfection, because organic matter consumes and shields against biocide. Cleaning then disinfection lets the biocide act effectively on clean surfaces.

n.1: Sediment protects micro-organisms from disinfectant rather than helping it work.
n.2: Disinfecting over debris wastes biocide and leaves shielded organisms.
n.3: Refilling without cleaning or disinfecting leaves a contaminated cistern in service.

5.q: Without a working secondary return, what tends to happen to hot water in long pipe runs?
o: It gets hotter and hotter the further it has to travel
It is somehow filtered completely clean of all bacteria
It turns into perfectly safe cold drinking water
It cools down and can drop into the legionella growth range
5.w: In long dead legs or runs without circulation, stationary hot water cools into the range where legionella multiply.

n.0: Water loses heat as it sits in pipes; it does not get hotter.
n.1: Cooling in the pipe does not remove bacteria; it encourages their growth.
n.2: It becomes tepid rather than a safe cold supply.

6.q: What is the approximate maximum blended temperature a TMV should deliver to a bath used by at-risk people?
o: About 50°C, which is the minimum required at a hot tap outlet
About 55°C, which is a typical hot water distribution temperature
About 60°C, which is the usual hot water storage temperature
About 43°C, the recognised upper blended limit for a bath
6.w: Delivery to baths for vulnerable users is limited to around 43°C as an upper figure to avoid scalding.

n.0: 50°C is above the safe blended limit and risks scalding.
n.1: 55°C is a distribution temperature, not a safe blended delivery figure.
n.2: 60°C is the storage temperature and would cause scalds quickly.

6.q: The responsible person is away on leave for two weeks. How should continuity of legionella control be maintained?
o: All monitoring simply stops until the responsible person returns
Control measures are suspended and then restarted on their return
The tasks pass to whoever happens to be on site that day
A trained and competent deputy is appointed to cover the duties
6.w: A competent deputy should be appointed so the control duties continue without a gap during absences.

n.0: Stopping monitoring during absence would break the control regime.
n.1: Suspending controls allows conditions for legionella to develop.
n.2: Duties should go to a competent deputy, not any untrained bystander.

6.q: If the risk assessment finds a foreseeable legionella risk, what must the duty holder put in place?
o: A notice telling users they may run the taps whenever they wish
Nothing further, because the assessment on its own is quite enough
A single verbal instruction given to staff on just one occasion
A written scheme of control setting out how the risk is managed
6.w: Where a risk is identified, a written scheme of control must be prepared describing how the risk is managed.

n.0: An informal notice does not meet the requirement for a written scheme of control.
n.1: The assessment alone is not enough; a written scheme is required when a risk is found.
n.2: A one-off verbal instruction is not a documented, controlled scheme.

6.q: What is the main reason a cold water storage tank must have a close-fitting lid?
o: To keep out light, dust, insects, debris and vermin
To raise the water pressure delivered around the building
To make the heavy tank easier to lift and move about
To stop the water inside from freezing during winter
6.w: A close-fitting lid keeps out light, dust, insects, debris and birds or vermin that would contaminate the stored water and encourage bacterial growth.

n.1: A lid has no effect on pressure, which comes from the tank's height.
n.2: A lid is a hygiene barrier, not a lifting aid; tanks are fixed.
n.3: Insulation, not the lid, protects against freezing.

6.q: Where are legionella bacteria commonly found in the natural environment?
o: In natural fresh water like rivers and lakes
Only in dry desert soil, never in wet places
Only inside people, not the wider environment
Only in salt water such as seas and oceans
6.w: Legionella occurs naturally in freshwater sources such as rivers, lakes and ground water, usually in low numbers.

n.3: They live mainly in fresh water, not salt water.
n.2: They live in the environment, not naturally inside people.
n.1: They need water to survive, so dry desert soil is not a typical source.

6.q: Which statement about where Legionella typically grows within a system is correct?
o: Only inside completely sealed pressure gauges
Only suspended free in fast-flowing water, never on surfaces
Mainly on inner surfaces, in biofilm, scale and sediment
Only in the open air above the water surface
6.w: Much Legionella growth occurs on wetted surfaces within biofilm and among scale and sediment, which shelter and feed it. Water sampling can under-represent this, so surfaces and deposits must be controlled.

n.0: It is not confined to sealed gauges; it colonises pipework, tanks and fittings.
n.1: Surfaces and biofilm are a primary habitat; the bacteria are not limited to flowing water.
n.3: Legionella is a waterborne organism that grows in the water and on wetted surfaces, not in open air above it.

6.q: Under HSG274 Part 2, how often should shower heads and hoses normally be cleaned, descaled and disinfected as a minimum?
o: Only when a user complains about the spray
Once every two years
At least quarterly (every three months)
Annually, at the same time as the tank inspection
6.w: HSG274 Part 2 recommends dismantling, cleaning, descaling and disinfecting shower heads and hoses at least every three months, because scale and biofilm accumulate quickly in these fittings.

n.1: A two-year interval would allow extensive scale and biofilm to build up in the head and hose between cleans.
n.0: Cleaning must be a planned, scheduled control, not something left until a user notices a problem.
n.3: Annual cleaning is far too infrequent for aerosol-generating fittings that foul rapidly.

6.q: You notice sediment has settled in the base of a large, slowly-used cold tank. Why does this raise the risk?
o: The sediment feeds bacteria while the slow turnover lets water stagnate and warm
A large tank turns its stored water over much faster than a small one
The settled sediment keeps the whole tank below 20°C and dormant
The settled sediment gradually disinfects the stored water
6.w: Settled sediment supplies nutrients while the slow, stagnant turnover lets numbers build up.

n.1: A large tank with low demand turns its water over more slowly, not faster.
n.2: Sediment does not keep water cold; it insulates and enriches it.
n.3: Debris harbours bacteria rather than disinfecting.

6.q: Organic matter such as leaves or dead insects getting into a water tank is a risk because it:
o: Adds extra nutrients that Legionella can feed and grow on
Cools the stored water to well below 20°C
Cannot affect the water quality in any way
Instantly kills all bacteria already present
6.w: Organic debris adds nutrients that help feed Legionella growth.

n.1: Debris does not cool water; it can enrich and slightly warm it.
n.2: Contamination of stored water is a genuine, well-known risk.
n.3: Debris feeds bacteria, it does not kill them.

6.q: During disinfection of a hot water system to a high temperature, why do TMVs need particular attention?
o: They may need isolating or set to pass hot water to disinfect their internals
They automatically raise the disinfection temperature at the outlet
They must be run at their normal blended setting to protect them from the heat
They should be removed entirely and refitted only after everything has cooled
6.w: TMVs will normally blend the hot disinfection water down, so they must be managed – isolated or set to pass hot water under controlled conditions – so their internals are disinfected while operators are protected from the hot flow.

n.1: A TMV lowers, not raises, the temperature reaching the outlet.
n.2: Left at the blended setting, the valve internals may not reach disinfection temperature.
n.3: Wholesale removal is not the standard approach; controlled isolation or bypass is used.

6.q: During the monthly round you notice a stored cold water tank reading of 24°C. What does this suggest?
o: The thermometer must be faulty, so the reading can safely be ignored
The cold water is warmer than it should be and needs reporting
The tank is perfectly within its normal working limits
Cold water sitting at 24°C is actually the safest of all
6.w: Cold water above 20°C is out of specification and must be recorded and reported so the cause can be found and fixed.

n.2: 24°C exceeds the 20°C cold-water limit, so it is not within limits.
n.0: Assuming the instrument is faulty and ignoring the result hides a possible real problem.
n.3: Warmer cold water favours legionella growth; it is not safest.

6.q: A cold water storage tank temperature is found to be rising toward the range where legionella can multiply. Whose job is it to make sure this is acted upon?
o: The water meter reader who calls to read the supply meter
The member of the public who reported feeling unwell that day
The HSE inspector whenever they next happen to visit
The responsible person, acting on the operative's report
6.w: The operative reports the finding and the responsible person ensures corrective action is taken.

n.0: A meter reader has no responsibility for the control scheme.
n.1: A member of the public has no role in managing the control scheme.
n.2: Action cannot wait for a possible future HSE visit.

6.q: SCENARIO: You check the calorifier and the stored hot water reads 54°C instead of the expected 60°C. What should you do?
o: Record it and report the low storage temperature to the responsible person
Adjust the risk assessment yourself so that it now allows a 54°C reading
Drain down the whole calorifier straight away without telling anybody first
Say nothing at all, as 54°C is surely close enough to be safe
6.w: Stored hot water below 60°C is out of specification and must be recorded and reported so the fault can be put right.

n.1: An operative cannot rewrite the risk assessment to accept an unsafe temperature.
n.2: Draining the vessel unilaterally is not an operative's decision.
n.3: 54°C is below the 60°C target and does not reliably control legionella.

6.q: Which of these is the strongest reason to remove rather than merely isolate a redundant pipe branch with a valve?
o: Isolation valves cost considerably more than simply removing the pipe
Valves always leak and cause flooding within a few days
An isolated branch raises the flow rate to all other outlets
The isolated branch still holds standing water that stagnates
6.w: Closing a valve leaves a stagnant, water-filled length beyond it. If the valve is later opened, or leaks by, that colonised water can enter the live system. Removal back to the live main eliminates the retained volume.

n.0: Cost is not the guidance reason; the retained stagnant water is.
n.1: Valves do not always leak within days; this is not the rationale.
n.2: Isolating a branch does not meaningfully raise flow to other outlets.

6.q: Part-way through a chlorination the measured disinfectant residual is well below the level required for the method. What should the operative do?
o: Assume it is close enough and move straight on to flushing
Complete the job anyway and record it as a normal and successful disinfection
Reduce the contact time to match the lower measured residual
Re-establish the required residual and hold it for the full contact time
6.w: The method depends on maintaining the required concentration for the contact time; if the residual drops, it must be brought back up and held for the full time before flushing.

n.0: Flushing before the residual is held leaves it inadequately disinfected.
n.1: Recording an under-dosed run as successful is inaccurate and unsafe.
n.2: Shortening the contact time undermines the disinfection, not fixes it.

6.q: Which situation best explains why a cold outlet might read 22°C despite the incoming mains being 12°C?
o: The cold pipe is warming, running near a hot pipe or warm space
The thermometer is faulty and adds ten degrees to every reading
The mains reading is wrong, as cold water cannot warm in pipework
Cold water is naturally warmer at outlets than the mains by design
6.w: Cold water warming above 20°C in distribution usually reflects heat gain, such as cold pipes routed near hot services or through warm risers; the cause should be investigated and reported.

n.1: A consistent physical cause is more likely than a fixed instrument offset.
n.2: Cold water certainly can warm in pipework; that is the risk being detected.
n.3: A rise into the danger zone is a fault, not by design.

6.q: Which of these correctly pairs the illness with its nature?
o: Legionnaires' disease is mild and self-limiting; Pontiac fever is a fatal severe pneumonia
Legionnaires' disease is a serious pneumonia; Pontiac fever is milder and self-limiting
Legionnaires' disease is a skin condition; Pontiac fever is a stomach infection
Both Legionnaires' disease and Pontiac fever are contagious chest infections
6.w: Legionnaires' disease is a serious, potentially fatal pneumonia, whereas Pontiac fever is the milder, self-limiting form of Legionella infection.

n.0: This reverses the two; Legionnaires' is the serious one.
n.2: Neither is a skin or stomach condition; both come from inhaled legionella.
n.3: Neither is contagious; legionella does not spread person to person.

6.q: When cutting back a redundant pipe, how close to the live main should the cut be made?
o: About one metre away from the main is close enough
As close as practicable so almost no dead length remains
Roughly halfway along the old branch
Right at the old outlet position only
6.w: Cutting back close to the live main leaves the shortest possible stub, minimising standing water.

n.0: A metre of pipe left on the main is still a dead leg holding stagnant water.
n.2: Cutting halfway leaves a long stagnant stub still connected.
n.3: Cutting at the old outlet removes nothing useful and leaves the whole branch as a dead leg.

6.q: When checking a calorifier for temperature control, why is the reading taken at the base of the vessel especially important?
o: The base is where the safety relief valve is fitted onto the vessel
The base of the vessel is always the very hottest point inside it
The base is the coolest point, so it confirms the whole volume has reached temperature
The base reading is only really needed in order to check the water pressure in the vessel
6.w: Because cooler water and sediment settle at the bottom, the base is typically the coldest point. Confirming it is at temperature verifies the entire stored volume, not just the hot upper layer, is being controlled.

n.0: The base check is about the coolest water, not the safety valve.
n.1: The base is normally the coolest point due to stratification.
n.3: The base check is about temperature, not pressure.

6.q: A responsible person suggests replacing routine temperature monitoring with occasional legionella sampling to save time. Why is this not acceptable?
o: Sampling gives an instant result right at the outlet, unlike the temperature checks on site
Sampling supplements temperature control but does not replace it as the main measure
Sampling is only ever used in cooling towers and never in hot and cold systems
Sampling is cheaper to carry out, so it should always be the primary method
6.w: HSG274 Part 2 is clear that microbiological sampling can supplement monitoring but is not a substitute for maintaining and checking temperature control, which remains the principal routine control.

n.0: Sampling results take days of laboratory culture, so they give no instant assurance.
n.2: Sampling can be used in hot and cold systems too, but as a supplement.
n.3: Cost does not make sampling the primary method; it is a supplementary check.

6.q: Staff are worried about scalding from hot taps. What is the correct way to control scald risk without lowering the calorifier storage temperature?
o: Remove the hot water supply from the entire building, leaving only cold
Turn the calorifier off completely between each use
Store the water at only 40°C in the calorifier
Fit thermostatic mixing valves at the outlets to blend the water down
6.w: Thermostatic mixing valves blend hot and cold at the point of use, controlling scald risk while storage stays safely hot.

n.2: Storing at 40°C would create ideal conditions for legionella.
n.1: Switching the calorifier off between uses lets the water cool into the growth range.
n.0: Removing the hot supply is not a practical or safe control for a working building.

6.q: A tank lid is made of a translucent plastic that lets daylight pass through into the tank. What should be done?
o: Fit a light-proof cover so daylight cannot reach the water
Add more water so that light cannot reach right to the bottom
Paint the inside of the tank black to block the light coming through
Leave it as it is, since a little daylight keeps the water fresh
6.w: Daylight reaching the water encourages algae and microbial growth, so the tank needs a light-proof lid or cover.

n.1: Extra water does not block light entering through a translucent lid and still allows growth near the surface.
n.2: Painting the inside adds a coating not approved for drinking water and does not stop light entering.
n.3: Light never keeps water fresh; it encourages micro-organisms to grow.

6.q: How often should shower heads and hoses be cleaned, descaled and disinfected as a minimum?
o: At least once every three months as a minimum
Once a year during the annual service visit
Once every two years when convenient
Only when they visibly look dirty or heavily scaled
6.w: Guidance recommends cleaning, descaling and disinfecting shower heads and hoses at least quarterly, that is every three months.

n.1: Yearly is far too infrequent to control scale and biofilm in a shower head.
n.2: Two years would allow heavy scale and bacterial growth to build up.
n.3: Waiting until it looks dirty is not acceptable; a routine quarterly schedule is required.

6.q: A colleague suggests writing down a temperature that was never actually measured to save time on the checks. What is the correct response?
o: Record the made-up figure but simply tell nobody about it
Only ever do it for the outlets that are genuinely hard to reach
Refuse; readings must be genuine and records must never be falsified
Agree to it, as long as the invented figure still looks perfectly reasonable
6.w: Records must be truthful; falsifying a check hides risk and is never acceptable.

n.0: Keeping quiet still leaves a dishonest, unsafe record in place.
n.1: Difficulty of access does not justify inventing a reading.
n.3: A plausible-looking invented figure is still a false record.

6.q: How long should records of the risk assessment and monitoring of control measures generally be retained?
o: For a suitable period, so trends can be reviewed and control demonstrated over time
Records are never really needed at all, as long as the water looks clear
Only until the end of the current working day, and then they are discarded
They may be destroyed the moment they have been written down on the sheet, if wished
6.w: L8 expects records to be kept for a suitable period so that the effectiveness of the scheme can be reviewed over time and compliance demonstrated; monitoring results in particular should be retained long enough to show trends.

n.1: Clear-looking water proves nothing; records are still required.
n.2: A single day is far too short to show whether control is being maintained.
n.3: Immediate destruction would defeat the purpose of recording and prevent trend review.

7.q: Why should a TMV be fitted as close as reasonably practicable to the outlet it serves?
o: To make the valve easier to reach for reading its serial number
To minimise the pipework holding tepid blended water where legionella grows
To reduce the pressure that the outlet fittings must withstand
To allow the blended supply to be shared between several buildings
7.w: Blended water sits in the legionella growth range, so the run of pipe carrying it must be kept as short as possible; siting the TMV close to the outlet minimises this dead-leg of tepid water.

n.0: Ease of reading a serial number is not the reason for close siting.
n.2: Positioning is about temperature and dead-legs, not outlet pressure ratings.
n.3: Blended supplies should serve only nearby outlets, not be distributed widely.

7.q: Which of the following best describes 'so far as is reasonably practicable' in the Health and Safety at Work Act?
o: Ignoring a risk whenever controlling it would be inconvenient to arrange
Balancing the level of risk against the time, trouble and cost of controlling it
Always choosing whatever option happens to be the cheapest available
Spending an unlimited amount of money no matter how small the risk
7.w: Reasonably practicable means weighing the level of risk against the effort and cost needed to control it.

n.0: Inconvenience does not excuse leaving a significant risk uncontrolled.
n.2: Cost cannot be put ahead of a serious risk; it is a balance, not the cheapest option.
n.3: The test is proportionate, not a requirement to spend without limit.

7.q: Why can a garden or site hose left lying in the sun be a legionella risk when next used?
o: Warm, still water inside lets legionella grow, then sprays out
A hose simply cannot hold any water inside its length
A hose can never produce any spray or fine mist
Sunlight somehow adds fresh legionella into the hose
7.w: Water trapped in a warm hose can let legionella multiply, and switching the hose on can then release a contaminated spray.

n.1: Hoses do retain water inside them.
n.3: Sunlight warms the water but does not 'add' bacteria to it.
n.2: A hose nozzle can readily produce a fine spray.

7.q: What is the correct arrangement of the cold feed (outlet) and the inlet on a storage cistern to encourage good mixing and turnover?
o: Inlet and outlet set so water flows across the cistern to the draw-off, avoiding dead zones
Inlet and outlet both fitted at the base so no fresh water reaches the surface
Inlet and outlet placed immediately next to each other on the same side
Outlet fitted at the very top so only the warmest surface water is drawn off
7.w: Positioning the inlet and outlet so water flows across the cistern promotes turnover and mixing, avoiding short-circuiting and stagnant dead zones where Legionella can develop.

n.1: Drawing only from the base leaves surface water stagnant and is poor practice.
n.2: Adjacent inlet and outlet short-circuit the flow, leaving most water stagnant.
n.3: Drawing only warm surface water leaves cooler water below stagnant.

7.q: Why is checking the fail-safe shut-off part of TMV maintenance?
o: To confirm the valve still stops the flow if the cold supply fails
To confirm the valve is still able to heat the water on demand quickly
To confirm the valve stores enough cold water in reserve
To confirm the valve changes colour whenever it runs hot
7.w: The fail-safe check proves the TMV will shut down if the cold supply is lost, so a user cannot be scalded by full-temperature water.

n.1: A TMV does not heat water, so this is not what is tested.
n.2: A TMV does not store cold water.
n.3: Colour change is not a TMV function or a maintenance check.

7.q: You find a spray tap in a washroom that is heavily scaled and barely spraying. What should you do?
o: Ignore it completely, since some water is still coming out
Turn the water pressure right up to try to force it through
Wrap some tape around the outlet to hide the scale from view
Clean and descale the tap fitting and strainer, then report it if a bigger fix is needed
7.w: A scaled spray fitting should be cleaned and descaled so it works properly and does not harbour bacteria, and reported if a bigger fix is needed.

n.0: Ignoring scale lets bacteria and biofilm build up further.
n.1: Raising pressure does not remove scale and may worsen aerosol.
n.2: Hiding the scale does nothing to control the risk.

7.q: Who should carry out cleaning and disinfection of a storage tank found to be contaminated?
o: Nobody, since tanks simply clean themselves over time
Any passer-by who happens to be available at the time
The first person to notice it, without any training at all
A competent, trained person following a safe procedure
7.w: Cleaning and disinfection must be done by a competent, trained person following a safe, controlled procedure so the work is effective and safe.

n.1: An untrained passer-by could do the job wrongly or unsafely.
n.0: Tanks do not self-clean; contamination remains until removed.
n.2: Noticing a problem does not make someone competent to carry out disinfection.

7.q: What is a flow straightener or strainer fitted in a spray tap or tap outlet?
o: A device that heats the water as it leaves the tap
A small insert at the outlet that shapes the flow and traps debris
A meter that records how much water has been used
A valve that stops water from flowing backwards
7.w: A flow straightener or strainer sits at the outlet to shape flow and can trap debris and scale, so it needs regular cleaning.

n.0: It does not heat water; it shapes and screens the flow.
n.2: It does not measure water use.
n.3: A backflow stop is a check valve, not a flow straightener.

7.q: You spot heavy rust and brown sludge in the bottom of a storage tank. Why is this a Legionella risk?
o: Rust and sludge have no measurable effect on bacteria in stored water
The rust and sludge feed and shelter the bacteria in the tank
The layer of rust keeps the stored water above 60°C at all times
The brown sludge sterilises the water and makes it safe to use
7.w: Rust and sludge provide nutrients and sheltered surfaces that help Legionella build up.

n.0: Corrosion and debris are recognised nutrient sources for Legionella.
n.2: Rust does not heat the water.
n.3: Sludge harbours bacteria rather than sterilising water.

7.q: A Legionella bacterium is a biological agent. Which regulations most directly require employers to assess and control the risk from exposure to it as a hazardous substance?
o: The Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015
The Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 1992
The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (COSHH)
7.w: COSHH covers hazardous substances including biological agents such as Legionella bacteria, requiring assessment and control of exposure. L8 and HSG274 give the practical guidance for meeting these duties.

n.0: CDM concerns management of construction projects, not control of Legionella.
n.1: The PPE Regulations cover protective equipment, not the substance risk assessment.
n.2: PUWER concerns the safety of work equipment, not a biological agent.

7.q: A calorifier is taken out of service for internal inspection and cleaning. Before opening it, the operative should first:
o: Add fresh sludge inside to protect the internal metal surfaces
Turn the storage temperature right up to 90°C before opening the vessel
Open the vessel up while it is still completely full and hot
Isolate and safely drain the vessel following the correct procedure
7.w: The calorifier must be isolated and safely drained down following the correct procedure before it can be opened for inspection.

n.0: Sludge is removed during cleaning, never added.
n.1: Raising the temperature does not prepare it and adds a burn hazard.
n.2: Opening a full, hot vessel is unsafe and risks scalding.

7.q: A maintenance team is about to open and flush a rarely used spray tap that has stood full of warm water for months. Why should they treat this task with particular care regarding Legionella?
o: Because the main danger is swallowing droplets rather than inhaling them
Because spray taps cannot make aerosols small enough to be inhaled
The first spray could release aerosols from water where bacteria may have multiplied
Because the water is certain to be safe after standing that long
7.w: Warm, stagnant water in a little-used spray tap can allow Legionella to multiply, and operating it can release aerosols the workers may inhale, so the task needs care.

n.0: The danger is inhaling the aerosol, not swallowing droplets.
n.1: Spray taps do produce fine, inhalable aerosols, which is the whole concern.
n.3: Long standing warm water is more likely to be contaminated, not safe.

7.q: Why is sludge and sediment at the base of a calorifier a concern?
o: It makes the stored water heat up far too quickly
It shelters legionella from the hot water above it
It improves the flow and return balance of the loop
It raises the storage temperature above 60°C on its own
7.w: Sludge and sediment settling at the base protect legionella and other bacteria from the heat of the stored water, so the base must be drained and de-sludged.

n.0: Sludge insulates and slows heat reaching the base; it does not speed heating.
n.2: Sludge worsens performance and hygiene; it does not improve balance.
n.3: Sludge does not raise storage temperature; it creates cool, sheltered layers.

7.q: When checking a TMV-served basin used by vulnerable people, which blended-outlet temperature would you expect to record as within the safe delivery range?
o: Around 41°C, within the typical safe blended range
At least 60°C to match the storage temperature
Below 20°C, as for a cold-only outlet
Exactly 50°C, the hot sentinel figure
7.w: TMVs deliver a blended temperature typically around 38-46°C to prevent scalding of vulnerable users; a recorded value near 41°C sits within that safe range.

n.1: 60°C at the outlet would scald; that figure is the storage temperature, not the blended delivery.
n.2: Below 20°C is a cold sentinel target and would be far too cold for a blended washing outlet.
n.3: 50°C is the hot sentinel control temperature, above the safe blended delivery range for a TMV outlet.

7.q: At what temperature should water be stored in a calorifier (hot water cylinder) to control Legionella?
o: Stored at 50°C or above at all times
Stored at around 55°C or slightly above
Stored at 70°C or above at all times
Stored at 60°C or above at all times
7.w: Hot water should be stored at 60°C or above to keep the bacteria from multiplying.

n.0: 50°C is the minimum at the outlet, not the storage temperature.
n.1: 55°C is below the required storage minimum of 60°C.
n.2: 70°C is higher than needed and risks scalding and energy waste.

7.q: What tends to happen to the temperature of water trapped in a long dead leg?
o: It always stays reliably below 20 degrees C, whatever the surroundings are
It stays at exactly the same temperature as the live main from which it branches off
It drifts towards the surrounding room temperature, often into the growth range
It always stays reliably above 60 degrees C, whatever the surroundings are
7.w: Trapped water loses or gains heat towards the ambient temperature, frequently landing in the 20-45 degrees C growth range.

n.0: It only stays cold if the surroundings are cold, often not the case.
n.1: Because it is not flowing, it drifts towards ambient, away from the main.
n.3: It only stays hot if kept hot; a dead leg normally cools down.

7.q: What is the written scheme of control (the written scheme) for?
o: To keep a running list of the names of everyone who has ever visited the site
To record only the total cost of the chemicals that were used
To advertise the building's facilities to prospective new tenants
To set out how the risk is prevented or controlled and managed safely
7.w: The written scheme describes the water system and sets out the measures to be taken to prevent or control the risk.

n.0: A visitor log has nothing to do with controlling legionella.
n.1: Chemical costs are not the purpose of the written scheme.
n.2: Marketing the building is unrelated to controlling the risk.

7.q: You reach a little-used guest bathroom hot tap that reads only 40°C after a minute. What is the best action?
o: Leave it as it is, since guests only very rarely use that bathroom
Record and report it, and consider regular flushing of the outlet
Turn up every calorifier across the whole site immediately
Cap the offending tap off yourself there and then
7.w: 40°C fails the 50°C minimum, so it is recorded, reported, and infrequent use is flagged for flushing.

n.0: Rare use makes stagnation more likely, so it cannot be ignored.
n.2: Turning up all calorifiers is not a targeted or safe response.
n.3: Capping outlets is not an operative's decision to take alone.

7.q: Standing water in a poorly used section of pipe has been found at 32 degrees C. What does this reading indicate for legionella control?
o: It is safely below the growth range, so no further action at all is needed here
It sits in the 20–45°C range that favours legionella multiplication and needs control
It is above the growth range, and so the legionella present is being killed off quickly
The temperature does not matter at all, provided the water still looks nice and clear
7.w: 32 degrees C is well within the 20-45 degrees C band in which legionella multiplies most readily; the stagnation and temperature together indicate a real risk requiring flushing, temperature control or removal of the section.

n.0: 32°C is inside, not below, the growth range.
n.2: Legionella is not killed until well above 50°C; 32°C encourages growth.
n.3: Clear-looking water can still be heavily colonised.

7.q: During a monitoring check you record a temperature reading that is outside the required range. What is the correct action?
o: Re-write the reading so that it falls neatly back within the range
Correct the reading only if somebody else happens to notice it later
Ignore it entirely, since a single reading is unlikely to matter
Record it, then escalate to the responsible person so the cause can be corrected
7.w: An out-of-range reading or fault must be recorded, escalated to the responsible person, and the underlying cause corrected; findings are never altered or ignored.

n.0: Altering a reading is falsification of a safety record and is never acceptable.
n.1: Correct handling does not depend on whether anyone notices; it must always be recorded.
n.2: An out-of-range reading is a sign of possible loss of control and must be acted on.

7.q: Why is sediment or sludge collecting at the base of a calorifier or cold water tank a particular concern for Legionella growth?
o: It settles out all the bacteria and safely removes them from the water
It provides both nutrients and shelter where legionella and biofilm can thrive
It has no bearing on growth, as bacteria live only in flowing water
It keeps the stored water held at a lethal temperature
7.w: Accumulated sludge, rust and sediment supply nutrients and a protected surface for biofilm, where Legionella multiplies and is shielded from temperature and disinfectant. Removing deposits by cleaning is a recognised control.

n.0: Settled sediment concentrates nutrients and bacteria rather than safely removing them.
n.2: Legionella thrives in stagnant, sediment-rich zones, not only in flowing water.
n.3: Sediment does not heat water; the base of a tank is often cooler and higher-risk.

7.q: What must an operative do before using a disinfectant they have not used before?
o: Read and understand the COSHH assessment and safety data sheet
Taste a small amount of the product to confirm it is still active
Mix it with another chemical to make it act stronger
Assume it behaves the same as every other chemical
7.w: Each chemical has its own hazards; the COSHH assessment and safety data sheet must be read and understood before use.

n.3: Different disinfectants have different hazards, dilutions and precautions.
n.1: Tasting a disinfectant is dangerous and never a valid test.
n.2: Mixing chemicals can create toxic gases and is strictly avoided unless specified.

7.q: When a monitoring result is out of specification, what must happen in addition to recording it?
o: It should be averaged with good readings to hide it
It should be left for next year's check to sort out
It must trigger remedial action and be escalated
It should be quietly deleted so the log stays clean
7.w: Out-of-specification results must lead to remedial action and be escalated to the responsible person.

n.0: Averaging a bad reading away conceals the problem instead of fixing it.
n.1: Leaving a fault for a year leaves the risk uncontrolled.
n.3: Deleting a failing result hides a genuine risk and falsifies records.

7.q: A hotel wants to fit TMVs on the guest bath taps in a wing used mainly by elderly holiday groups. What temperature should the baths be set to deliver?
o: Around 55°C to match the distribution temperature
Around 30°C so it is never warm enough to scald
Around 41°C, safely below the scalding threshold
Around 60°C to match storage
7.w: A blended bath delivery of about 41°C is warm and comfortable while staying safely below the scalding threshold for older guests.

n.0: 55°C is a distribution temperature and would scald.
n.3: 60°C is the storage temperature and would cause rapid scalds.
n.1: 30°C is too cool for a comfortable bath and is not what TMVs are set to.

7.q: Which statement best reflects how often a Legionella risk assessment should be reviewed?
o: Regularly, and also whenever there is reason to suspect it is no longer valid
Just the once when it is first written down, and then never looked at again at all
Strictly every ten years to the exact day, and at no other time
Only if a member of the public makes a formal written complaint
7.w: L8 expects periodic review and, on top of that, review whenever there is reason to think the assessment is no longer valid — such as changes to the system, its use, or a suspected case of disease.

n.1: A one-off assessment cannot stay valid as systems and uses change over time.
n.3: A public complaint is not the only, or main, trigger for review.
n.2: There is no fixed ten-year rule; review is driven by suitability and change.

8.q: Why is legionella specifically covered by COSHH?
o: Because it is a biological agent that is hazardous to health
Because it is a highly flammable liquid stored on the premises
Because it is a controlled explosive requiring a licence
Because it is classed as a road transport hazard in transit
8.w: Legionella bacteria are a biological agent hazardous to health, which brings them within COSHH.

n.1: Legionella is a living organism, not a flammable liquid.
n.2: It is not an explosive substance.
n.3: COSHH covers it as a health hazard, unrelated to transport rules.

8.q: A duty-holder wants to protect users from scalding at wash-hand basins in a care home without lowering the stored hot water temperature. What is the correct approach?
o: Reduce the temperature at the calorifier down to 48°C during the night only in daily use
Fit thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) at the outlets to blend the hot water down
Remove the hot water supply from the wash-hand basins in the home entirely
Insulate the pipework so that the hot water cools before it reaches the tap
8.w: Scald protection is delivered at the point of use with TMVs, which blend stored 60°C water down to a safe temperature at the tap while storage and distribution stay hot for legionella control.

n.0: Dropping the calorifier to 48°C breaches the storage standard and risks growth.
n.2: Removing the hot supply is impractical and does not address safe warm-water delivery.
n.3: Insulation keeps water hot; it does not cool it.

8.q: What should be checked and cleaned on a spray tap besides the visible nozzle?
o: The decorative wall tiles behind and around the tap
The strainer or flow straightener where debris collects
Only the outer tap handle that the user actually turns
The waste pipe running away underneath the basin sink
8.w: The strainer or flow straightener collects debris and scale and must be cleaned as well as the visible nozzle.

n.0: Wall tiles are not part of the outlet's water hygiene.
n.2: Cleaning only the handle misses the parts in the water path.
n.3: The waste pipe is separate from the outlet fitting being cleaned.

8.q: You open a cold water tank lid and find dead insects, silt and a film of algae on the water. What should you do?
o: Put the lid back and leave it until the next yearly check comes round
Add some extra insulation to the tank and simply move on
Report it and arrange for the tank to be cleaned and disinfected
Skim off the bits you can see and then take no further action at all
8.w: Insects, silt and algae mean the tank is contaminated, so it must be reported and properly cleaned and disinfected.

n.0: Leaving known contamination lets legionella grow unchecked.
n.1: Insulation does not remove the contamination already in the tank.
n.3: Skimming the surface leaves the underlying contamination behind.

8.q: Why does scale build-up from hard water inside a pipe or fitting contribute to Legionella growth?
o: Scale provides surface area and nutrients that harbour biofilm and shelter bacteria
Scale raises the water temperature above 60°C and completely sterilises it
Scale dissolves the surrounding biofilm and starves the bacteria of nutrients
Scale prevents any water from ever contacting the inside of the pipe wall
8.w: Scale creates a rough surface and, with rust and sediment, forms deposits where biofilm establishes and Legionella shelters and feeds. Removing scale and sediment is part of controlling growth under HSG274 Part 2.

n.1: Scale does not heat water; it insulates surfaces and can even protect bacteria from heat.
n.2: Scale supports biofilm rather than dissolving it, so it encourages growth.
n.3: Scale is a deposit water flows over and around; it does not seal the bacteria away from water.

8.q: Which condition below is a recognised higher-risk factor for legionella infection?
o: Wearing glasses
Having brown hair
Diabetes
Being tall
8.w: Diabetes is a recognised underlying condition that increases vulnerability to serious Legionnaires' disease.

n.0: Wearing glasses is not a health risk factor for legionella.
n.1: Hair colour has no effect on infection risk.
n.3: Height is unrelated to susceptibility.

8.q: Why should the person managing the scheme be told promptly about a temperature reading that is out of range?
o: So the faulty thermometer can be blamed for the poor reading
So the monitoring log can simply be closed off for the whole year
So the out-of-range reading can be quietly ignored and forgotten
So corrective action can be taken quickly before the risk grows
8.w: Prompt reporting lets the responsible person act quickly to bring the control back on target before risk increases.

n.0: Blaming the instrument does not correct the water risk.
n.1: Closing the log does not address the failed control.
n.2: Ignoring an out-of-range reading leaves the risk uncontrolled.

8.q: A landlord suggests fitting TMVs to every outlet in an office block 'to be safe'. Why is this not the right approach?
o: Fitting TMVs to every single outlet would push the delivered water temperature far too high
Each TMV adds legionella risk and upkeep, so fit only where a scald risk justifies it
Offices are simply not permitted to have any hot water supply at all
TMVs are actually completely illegal to install in any office premises
8.w: Because a TMV is itself a legionella risk, valves are fitted only where vulnerable users create a genuine scald risk, not everywhere.

n.0: TMVs lower, not raise, the delivered temperature.
n.2: Offices are permitted hot water; the point is not to over-fit valves.
n.3: TMVs are not illegal in offices; they are simply not always needed.

8.q: As part of cold water monitoring, why is the incoming supply temperature also recorded where practicable?
o: To confirm the mains water meets the minimum drinking-water fluoride levels required
To set a baseline and reveal if the cold system is warming above the incoming value
To decide the correct colour coding for the cold pipework in the plant room
To help calculate the building's total metered water bill for the quarter
8.w: Recording the incoming cold temperature provides a baseline; a rise between the supply and outlets shows the system is picking up unwanted heat, which needs investigation.

n.0: Fluoride and drinking-water chemistry are separate from temperature monitoring.
n.2: Pipe colour coding follows standards, not the incoming temperature.
n.3: Billing is unrelated to temperature monitoring for legionella control.

8.q: An infrequently used outlet is identified during a review of a system. As a remedial control measure to reduce stagnation, the usual action is to:
o: Leave it unused, as unused outlets pose no risk
Cap it and forget about it without any record
Flush it regularly, or remove it if it is genuinely not needed
Increase the water temperature across the whole building instead
8.w: Little-used outlets allow water to stagnate; the remedial action is to flush them regularly to maintain turnover, or to remove redundant ones so they cannot become a source of contamination.

n.1: Capping without record leaves a dead leg that can still hold stagnant water; removal or managed flushing is preferred.
n.3: Raising temperature everywhere does not address stagnation in a specific unused outlet.
n.0: Unused outlets are a recognised risk because water stagnates in them; they must be managed.

8.q: An operative is asked to record 'sentinel' outlets for temperature monitoring. In relation to stagnation, which outlets are typically most useful to include?
o: Only the single outlet that is nearest the incoming main, whatever its level of use
Only those outlets that happen to be used continuously all day long
The furthest and nearest outlets to the source, plus low-use or long-branch ones
Any three of the outlets chosen completely at random each and every month
8.w: Sentinel outlets are usually the nearest and furthest points on a system, chosen to represent temperature control across it; including known low-use or long-branch outlets targets the places where stagnation and temperature drift are most likely.

n.0: A single near outlet does not represent the far, higher-risk parts of the system.
n.1: Continuously used outlets are least likely to stagnate and are not the priority.
n.3: Random monthly selection undermines trend monitoring and may miss high-risk points.

8.q: A school has a row of washbasins used by young children. Where should scald protection be applied?
o: By fitting TMVs at the basins while keeping the stored water hot
By removing the hot taps from all of the basins
By lowering the whole hot water supply down to 40°C
By running the basins from a rainwater collection butt
8.w: TMVs at the children's basins give safe warm water while the stored hot water stays at a temperature that controls legionella.

n.1: Removing hot taps leaves no warm water and does not control legionella.
n.2: Lowering the whole supply to 40°C sits in the legionella growth range.
n.3: Rainwater is not a suitable or safe supply for washbasins.

8.q: A cold water storage tank reads 21°C during a routine check. What is the correct interpretation?
o: It should be ignored, as storage tanks are exempt from checks
It is acceptable because 21°C is very near to 20°C
It is too cold and the stored water now needs heating
It is above the 20°C limit, so it must be recorded and then reported
8.w: At 21°C the stored cold water exceeds the 20°C limit and must be recorded and reported.

n.0: Tanks are included in the monitoring, not exempt.
n.1: Near the limit is not the same as meeting it.
n.2: Cold water is not required to be heated.

8.q: Which description of Legionnaires' disease is accurate?
o: A contagious chest cold passed between people by coughing
A mild throat infection that always clears without treatment
A potentially fatal form of pneumonia caused by legionella
A stomach bug spread by swallowing contaminated drinking water
8.w: Legionnaires' disease is a potentially fatal pneumonia (lung infection) caused by Legionella bacteria inhaled in contaminated aerosols.

n.0: It is not contagious and does not spread between people.
n.1: It is a serious pneumonia that can be fatal, not a mild throat infection.
n.3: It is not a stomach bug and is not caught by swallowing water.

8.q: A cold water outlet is reading above the temperature at which cold water should be kept. As remedial action, the operative should first:
o: Run the hot tap right next to it for a good while to compensate for it
Insulate the outlet handle so it feels cooler to the touch
Record it, report it and investigate the cause such as nearby warming
Ignore it, because cold water taps are always a low risk
8.w: A cold outlet running too warm is out of range, so it is recorded, reported and the cause (such as heat gain) investigated and corrected.

n.0: Running the hot tap adds heat nearby and does not address the warm cold-water problem.
n.1: Insulating the handle does nothing about the temperature of the water.
n.3: Warm cold-water is within the growth range, so it is not low risk.

8.q: Which combination best describes a well-managed cold water storage tank?
o: Close-fitting lid, intact screens, insulated, inspected
Open top, no screens, in a warm location, cleaned once a decade
Translucent lid, torn screens, sited right beside the hot boiler
Oversized, always full, uninsulated and never once inspected
8.w: A well-managed tank has a close-fitting light-proof lid, intact insect screens, adequate insulation, clean water and regular inspection, all of which control bacterial growth.

n.1: An open, unscreened tank in a warm spot invites contamination.
n.2: A translucent lid, torn screens and heat are all faults.
n.3: An oversized, uninsulated, uninspected tank stagnates and warms.

8.q: To confirm a calorifier is not stratified, what should be true of the stored water?
o: The water should be cooler at the outlet than the base
Only the base needs to be hot where sludge sits
The whole cylinder, from top to bottom, reaches a safe temperature
Only the very top of the cylinder needs to be hot
8.w: Avoiding stratification means the entire cylinder from top to bottom reaches a safe temperature, leaving no cool layers.

n.3: A hot top with a cool base is exactly the stratification to be avoided.
n.1: A cool top over a hot base is still stratified and unsafe.
n.0: The outlet should not be cooler; cool layers are the hazard.

8.q: Why does biofilm make Legionella harder to control?
o: It shields the bacteria from disinfectant and heat
It raises the water temperature above 60°C
It makes the bacteria die within a few minutes
It strips every last nutrient out of the water
8.w: Biofilm shields Legionella from disinfectant and from temperature swings, making control harder.

n.1: Biofilm does not heat the water.
n.2: Biofilm protects the bacteria, helping them survive.
n.3: Biofilm supplies nutrients rather than removing them.

8.q: A tap in an outbuilding is fed by a very long pipe from the main building. What temperature problem is likely?
o: Both hot and cold arrive far colder than intended
Cold arrives warmer and hot arrives cooler than intended
The delivered temperatures are unaffected by the pipe length
Both hot and cold arrive far hotter than intended
8.w: Over a long run the cold gains heat and the hot loses it, so both can drift towards the growth range.

n.0: The cold does not get colder over a long run; it warms up.
n.3: The hot does not get hotter; it cools down over distance.
n.2: Long runs clearly do affect the delivered temperatures.

8.q: A washroom spray tap sprays unevenly and spits. What is the most likely hygiene-related cause an operative should check?
o: The sink beneath the tap is too small
The mirror above the tap is loose
Scale or debris blocking the strainer or spray outlet
The tap is fitted in the wrong colour
8.w: Uneven spitting spray is commonly caused by scale or debris in the strainer or outlet, which should be cleaned.

n.0: Sink size does not affect the spray pattern.
n.1: A loose mirror is unrelated to the tap's flow.
n.3: Colour has nothing to do with how it sprays.

8.q: A nursery asks why it cannot simply run all its taps cool from the tank to avoid scalding toddlers. What should you explain?
o: Running the taps cool saves water and completely removes all of the risk
Cool stored water lets legionella grow; keep storage hot and fit TMVs at the taps
Cool water straight from the tank is perfectly safe and needs no controls
Toddlers are not really at risk from hot water, so no controls are needed
8.w: Storing or standing water in the tepid range encourages legionella, so the system stays hot and TMVs temper the water at the point of use.

n.0: Running taps cool does not remove the legionella risk.
n.2: Cool stored water is a legionella risk, not automatically safe.
n.3: Toddlers are highly vulnerable to scalding, so protection is needed.

8.q: Hot water should reach what temperature at the sentinel taps within one minute of running?
o: It should reach 50°C or above at the tap
It should reach below 20°C at the tap
It should reach roughly 45°C at the tap
It should reach only around 30°C at the tap
8.w: Hot water should reach 50°C or above at the outlet within one minute to confirm the distribution temperature is being maintained.

n.1: Below 20°C would indicate no hot water control at all.
n.2: 45°C is short of the 50°C the outlet should reach.
n.3: 30°C sits within the legionella growth range.

8.q: What does the term 'suitable and sufficient' mean when applied to a risk assessment?
o: It is kept as brief as possible, deliberately leaving out almost all detail
It properly identifies the risks and the measures needed to control them
It is copied word for word from a completely different building
It simply lists all of the equipment installed across the site
8.w: A suitable and sufficient assessment properly identifies the significant risks and the control measures required.

n.0: An assessment must contain enough detail to be useful, not be deliberately brief.
n.2: A copied generic assessment may not reflect the actual system and its risks.
n.3: Listing equipment alone does not assess how the risk arises or is controlled.

8.q: A hot sentinel outlet on a hospital ward reads 51°C after running for a full minute. What is the correct interpretation and action?
o: It fails the 55°C healthcare standard, so record and report it
It is borderline but acceptable, so record it and take no action
It passes, because any reading above 50°C is acceptable everywhere
It passes, because a ward reading only needs to beat cold-water limits
8.w: Healthcare outlets must reach 55°C within one minute; 51°C is below that, so the reading is out of range and must be recorded and reported to the responsible person for investigation.

n.1: A reading below the required standard is a failure, not borderline.
n.2: The 50°C threshold is for general buildings; healthcare needs 55°C.
n.3: Cold-water limits are irrelevant; the 55°C hot standard applies.

8.q: The risk assessment and written scheme should be kept how?
o: Written once when first produced and then never changed again
Recorded and kept up to date to match the current system
Held only in the memory of one experienced member of staff
Shredded at the end of the first year to save on storage
8.w: Records must be kept and updated so the assessment and scheme always reflect the current system and controls.

n.0: An unchanged document soon fails to match a changing system.
n.2: Relying on memory leaves nothing others can follow or audit.
n.3: Destroying the records loses the basis for managing the risk.

9.q: Why does a long hot water pipe run to a distant outlet raise legionella risk?
o: The hot water gets even hotter and scalds the pipe
Long runs always keep the water above 60°C throughout
Long runs are said to remove all bacteria before water arrives
The water cools as it travels and enters the growth range
9.w: Over a long run, hot water loses heat and can drop into the 20-45 degrees C range where legionella grows.

n.0: Hot water loses heat over distance; it does not gain it.
n.1: Long runs tend to let hot water cool below target, not stay above 60°C.
n.2: Cooling in a long run does not sterilise the water; it can make matters worse.

9.q: Why should an operative understand the site's written scheme of control before starting work?
o: So they can justify charging the customer a higher price for the job
So they can decide for themselves that the whole scheme is unnecessary here
So they are able to change the system's control temperatures as they see fit
So they carry out the correct tasks in the correct way and know what to report
9.w: Understanding the scheme ensures tasks are done correctly and that faults are recognised and reported properly.

n.0: The scheme controls risk; it is not about adjusting charges.
n.1: The scheme is a legal control measure, not something an operative can dismiss.
n.2: Changing control temperatures is a decision for the responsible person.

9.q: Why should a report of 'flu that turned into pneumonia' in someone who recently used a suspect water system be taken seriously?
o: Because this progression fits Legionnaires' disease and needs investigation
Because only people who feel ill within an hour need worry
Because flu and Legionnaires' disease can never be confused
Because pneumonia after exposure is completely impossible
9.w: Flu-like symptoms progressing to pneumonia after exposure to a suspect water system fit the recognised pattern of Legionnaires' disease and should be investigated.

n.2: Early Legionnaires' disease can resemble flu, so they can indeed be confused, which is why it must be taken seriously.
n.3: Progression to pneumonia is exactly what can occur, not an impossibility.
n.1: Symptoms typically appear over 2 to 10 days, not within an hour.

9.q: A strainer or filter is often fitted on the inlets to a TMV. What is its purpose?
o: To add a dose of disinfectant into the blended water supply
To slow the flow right down so the water cools
To catch debris and grit that could stop the valve working
To gently warm the incoming cold water first
9.w: Inlet strainers trap debris so it cannot jam the valve or affect the blended temperature, and they must be cleaned during servicing.

n.3: A strainer does not heat the cold water.
n.0: A strainer does not dose disinfectant.
n.1: A strainer removes debris; it is not there to cool the water.

9.q: For how long should legionella monitoring, inspection and maintenance records generally be retained?
o: At least five years
Until the next monthly check is completed
Only while the current operative remains employed on site
Six months, then destroyed to save storage
9.w: ACOP L8 and HSG274 advise keeping records of the risk assessment, control scheme and monitoring for a suitable period, commonly at least five years.

n.1: Overwriting or discarding records each month destroys the audit trail entirely.
n.3: Six months is well short of the recommended retention period and would not support an investigation.
n.2: Retention is tied to a defined period, not to the tenure of any individual staff member.

9.q: A café installs a new decorative water feature that produces a fine spray in the seating area. What should happen to the legionella risk assessment?
o: It should be deleted, as the feature is only decorative
Nothing changes, as it only holds a small amount of water
It should be reviewed because a new aerosol-producing source is present
It should be swapped for the building's fire risk assessment
9.w: Adding new plant that creates aerosols is a relevant change, so the assessment must be reviewed to cover the new source.

n.0: Being decorative does not remove the aerosol risk.
n.1: Even a small volume of sprayed water can carry legionella.
n.3: A fire assessment does not address legionella at all.

9.q: Why is sludge at the base of a calorifier a particular concern for legionella control?
o: It improves the flow of hot water reaching the taps upstairs
It makes the stored water hotter than it was ever intended to be
It has no effect on legionella in the calorifier at all
It can shelter legionella and provide nutrients for them
9.w: Sludge and sediment shelter legionella and provide nutrients, protecting the bacteria from heat.

n.0: Sludge restricts and fouls the system rather than improving flow.
n.1: Sludge does not raise the water temperature; it insulates cooler pockets.
n.2: Sludge harbours bacteria, so it does have an effect.

9.q: An outlet has been disconnected and will never be used again. What should happen to the pipework serving it?
o: Remove the redundant pipework so it cannot become a dead leg
Leave it fully in place but make sure to flush it every week
Fill the whole pipe with disinfectant and seal up both ends
Leave it capped near the main so that it can be reused later on
9.w: Permanently redundant pipework should be removed so it does not sit as a dead leg where stagnant water lets legionella grow.

n.1: Flushing a pipe that will never be used is not the answer; remove it instead.
n.2: Sealing stagnant water in the pipe still leaves a dead leg harbouring bacteria.
n.3: A capped stub left on the main is exactly the dead leg that should be removed.

9.q: A thermometer pocket (test point) is fitted to the flow and return of a calorifier primarily to:
o: To provide a convenient point for adding biocide chemicals into the loop
To let trapped air escape from the circulation loop
To allow accurate temperature readings without opening up the system
To reduce the water pressure in the return pipe
9.w: Thermometer pockets let an operative insert a probe and take accurate flow and return readings quickly and safely, without breaking into the pipework, supporting routine monthly monitoring.

n.0: Test pockets are for temperature measurement, not for dosing chemicals into the system.
n.1: Air is vented through dedicated vents, not through a thermometer pocket.
n.3: A thermometer pocket does not regulate or reduce pressure in the return.

9.q: A monitoring reading is on the edge of the acceptable range and the operative is unsure whether it passes. The best action is to:
o: Round the figure right down to a clear fail and then simply leave it
Round it up to a clear pass so that the record looks fine
Do not record it at all until they are completely certain of it
Record the actual reading and check the scheme, then escalate if still unsure
9.w: The true reading is recorded and, where its meaning is unclear, the operative checks the scheme and escalates rather than guessing.

n.0: Rounding to a fail misrepresents the measured value.
n.1: Rounding to a pass falsifies the reading and may hide a problem.
n.2: Delaying the record risks the reading being forgotten or the entry missed.

9.q: When measuring the temperature at a mixed (blended) outlet fitted with a TMV, what should the operative bear in mind?
o: The blended temperature is deliberately reduced, so hot control is checked upstream
The blended outlet reading is the true test of hot water storage control
The blended reading replaces the need to check the incoming hot supply
A blended outlet should still reach 60°C to prove Legionella control
9.w: A TMV lowers the delivery temperature for scald safety, so a blended outlet will not read the hot control temperature; the hot supply must be checked upstream of the valve.

n.1: A blended reading reflects the mixed output, not the hot storage control temperature.
n.2: The blended reading does not replace an upstream hot-supply check.
n.3: Requiring 60°C at a blended tap would defeat the TMV's scald-prevention purpose.

9.q: An operative is asked to carry out a task that is not covered by their training and is not in the written scheme. What should they do?
o: Guess a sensible method and press on with it to save some time
Refuse to ever carry out any water work again in the future
Stop and get competent help or instruction before continuing
Do it in their own way and simply not record it at all
9.w: Operatives must work within their competence and the written scheme, seeking competent help rather than improvising on unfamiliar tasks.

n.0: Guessing on a safety-critical task risks contamination and harm.
n.1: The issue is this specific task, not all future work; total refusal over-reacts.
n.3: Working unrecorded outside the scheme breaches the control arrangements.

9.q: Scenario: An operative is unsure whether a task they have been given falls within the site's written scheme or their own competence. What is the legally and professionally correct action before proceeding?
o: Proceed anyway and interpret the scheme however seems fine
Stop and clarify the task with the responsible person first
Carry out a different task instead without recording it
Refuse to communicate and simply leave the site without notice
9.w: Where scope or competence is unclear, the correct action is to stop and clarify with the responsible person, consistent with the duty to work within the scheme and to take reasonable care.

n.0: Proceeding on personal interpretation risks working outside competence and the scheme.
n.2: Substituting an unrecorded task neither resolves the uncertainty nor meets record and reporting duties.
n.3: Leaving without notice abandons the task and fails the duty to communicate and cooperate.

9.q: Besides suitable temperature, which combination of conditions most favours Legionella multiplication?
o: High pressure running through completely sterile, deposit-free pipework
Frequent draw-off and a total absence of any deposits at all
Fast continuous flow with freshly chlorinated incoming water
Stagnation together with nutrients such as scale, rust, sludge and organic matter
9.w: Legionella needs warmth plus stagnant water and nutrients. Scale, rust, sludge, sediment and organic matter feed the bacteria and support biofilm, so still, dirty water in the growth range is highest risk.

n.0: High pressure and sterile pipework do not provide the stagnation and nutrients needed.
n.1: Frequent draw-off and clean pipework work against growth.
n.2: Continuous flow and disinfectant residual suppress growth rather than promoting it.

9.q: Regarding sex, who is statistically more likely to get Legionnaires' disease?
o: There is no difference at all
Men more than women
Women more than men
Only children
9.w: Men are affected by Legionnaires' disease more often than women.

n.2: The pattern is the reverse; men are affected more often.
n.0: There is a recognised difference, with men more affected.
n.3: It mainly affects adults, not principally children.

9.q: Why is simply capping off a disused pipe not good enough?
o: Caps are illegal fittings and are not permitted on water systems
A fitted cap will always begin to leak within just a few days
Capping the branch raises the system water pressure dangerously
The capped length still holds standing water that stagnates and grows legionella
9.w: A cap seals the end but the water trapped behind it becomes a stagnant dead leg.

n.0: Caps are commonly used fittings and are not illegal.
n.1: A properly fitted cap does not necessarily leak.
n.2: Capping a short branch does not create a dangerous pressure rise.

9.q: How often should the condition of a cold water storage tank normally be inspected as a minimum?
o: Once every five years
Once every ten years
At least once a year
Only when a fault is reported
9.w: Tanks should be inspected at least annually to check for debris, corrosion, a secure lid, light ingress and water clarity and temperature.

n.0: Five yearly is far too infrequent for a stored water tank.
n.3: Waiting for a fault means problems go unnoticed until it is too late.
n.1: Ten yearly leaves the tank unchecked for a dangerously long time.

9.q: How should a temperature monitoring record ideally be kept?
o: In writing, dated, showing outlet, reading and any action taken
Only in the operative's memory until the next site visit comes round
As a rough guess written in at the end of each month
On a loose scrap of paper that is thrown away after the visit
9.w: Records should be written, dated and show the outlet, reading and any action, to prove control.

n.1: Memory is not an auditable record.
n.2: Guessed retrospective figures are not valid records.
n.3: Discarded notes provide no evidence of monitoring.

9.q: A gym adds a new communal shower block used by many members each day. What should the water safety arrangements do?
o: Only assess the showers if member attendance starts to fall
Exclude the showers from the scheme because they are used so often
Cover the new showers in the assessment and scheme, since they create aerosols
Treat the new showers exactly the same as the outdoor car park
9.w: New showers generate aerosols and are heavily used, so they must be brought into the assessment and control scheme.

n.0: Falling attendance would raise stagnation risk, not remove the need to assess.
n.1: Frequent use reduces stagnation but does not remove the aerosol risk.
n.3: A car park has no water aerosol risk to compare with.

9.q: After first installing and setting a TMV, when is an early performance check commonly made?
o: Never again at all once the valve has first been set up
Soon after commissioning, then at regular intervals
A full ten years after it was first installed on site
Only once the valve has completely failed in service
9.w: An early check soon after commissioning, followed by regular checks, confirms the valve is holding its safe set temperature.

n.0: A set-and-never-check approach ignores temperature drift over time.
n.2: A ten-year gap is far too long for a safety-critical valve.
n.3: Waiting for total failure risks scalding before it is caught.

9.q: A responsible person asks why capped-off but still-connected shower branches are unacceptable. What is the best explanation?
o: They just make the wall behind them look rather untidy
They increase the water pressure to everywhere else
They form dead legs where water stagnates and legionella can grow
They are perfectly acceptable as long as the cap fitted is a brass one
9.w: A capped branch still full of water is a dead leg: the water sits stagnant, can warm up and grow Legionella, and organisms can migrate into the live supply, so redundant branches should be cut back to the main, not just capped.

n.0: Appearance is irrelevant; the objection is the stagnant dead leg it creates.
n.1: A capped dead leg does not usefully raise system pressure; the hazard is stagnation.
n.3: The material of the cap does not remove the dead-leg hazard behind it.

9.q: An entry shows a temperature reading but no operative's name or initials against it. Why does this weaken the record?
o: There is no traceability for who took the reading or whether to trust it
It stops the water supplier from issuing a compliance certificate for the site
It makes the ink much harder to read on the page later
It prevents the reading from being converted into Fahrenheit
9.w: Without identifying who took a reading, the record loses traceability and accountability, so its reliability cannot be assured during review or investigation.

n.2: Legibility of ink is unrelated to the missing accountability information.
n.3: Unit conversion is unaffected by whether a name is present.
n.1: Water suppliers do not issue certificates from these internal logs; the issue is traceability.

9.q: Which combination of materials and finish is appropriate for a cold water storage cistern used for wholesome (potable) water?
o: Galvanised steel fitted with an internal copper heating coil
WRAS-approved, non-corroding materials suitable for potable water
Reclaimed timber lined internally with heavy-duty plastic sheeting
Untreated mild steel finished with a bituminous internal coating
9.w: Cisterns should be made from WRAS-approved, non-corroding materials suitable for contact with potable water, so they do not taint the water or shed corrosion products.
