n.0: A heating coil warms the stored water, the opposite of keeping cold water below 20°C.
n.2: Improvised timber and sheeting are not approved potable-water materials.
n.3: Untreated mild steel corrodes and sheds rust; ad-hoc bituminous coatings are unsuitable.

9.q: What is the purpose of a screen fitted to a tank's air vent?
o: To stop the stored water gradually evaporating from the tank
To let air in and out while keeping insects and dust out
To reduce the noise made as the water fills the tank
To filter limescale out of the incoming mains supply
9.w: A vent screen allows the tank to breathe as the level changes while preventing insects, dust and debris from entering through the vent.

n.0: A closed lid limits evaporation; the vent screen excludes contaminants.
n.2: A screen is a hygiene barrier, not a noise reducer.
n.3: Vent screens do not treat mains water or remove limescale.

9.q: Which set of conditions in a building water system raises Legionella risk?
o: Fast-flowing water with no dead legs anywhere in the pipework runs
Warm cold-water, cool hot-water, and underused oversized pipework
Clean, well-used outlets that are flushed thoroughly every day
Cold water kept below 20°C and hot water kept above 60°C throughout
9.w: Warm cold-water, cool hot-water and oversized underused systems all push water into risky conditions.

n.0: Good flow and no dead legs reduce risk.
n.2: Regularly used and flushed outlets are lower risk.
n.3: Cold below 20°C and hot above 60°C are the correct control temperatures.

10.q: You find a capped, disused pipe branch that stays warm to the touch and is full of standing water. What should you do?
o: Open the cap to let the standing water drain onto the floor
Leave it as it is, because it already has a cap on the end
Add more lagging to the branch and take no other action
Report it and arrange for the deadleg to be removed
10.w: A warm, water-filled capped branch is a stagnant deadleg, so it should be reported and removed back to the live main.

n.0: Draining onto the floor is unsafe and does not remove the deadleg.
n.1: A cap does not fix the problem; the stagnant water remains inside.
n.2: Lagging alone leaves the stagnant water and deadleg in place.

10.q: Why should the cold water storage cistern feed the system so that water is drawn off and replaced regularly (good turnover)?
o: So the cistern can then quite safely be left completely uncovered without any risk at all
So fresh, cooler mains water regularly replaces the stored water, limiting stagnation
So protective scale forms faster and coats the base of the cistern
So that a much smaller and far cheaper float valve can be fitted to the cistern inlet
10.w: Regular turnover means stored water is frequently replaced with fresh, cooler mains water, reducing residence time, stagnation and the temperature rise that favour Legionella.

n.0: Good turnover does not remove the need for a close-fitting cover.
n.2: Scale is a contaminant to be removed, not encouraged.
n.3: Turnover is about water quality, not float valve cost.

10.q: A worker insists they 'definitely caught Legionnaires' from a workmate who had it last week'. Why is this explanation incorrect?
o: Because a workmate's illness would make the worker immune, not ill
Because only cooling towers, never any other source, can cause infection
Because the incubation period is far too short for that to happen
Because Legionnaires' disease is not spread from person to person
10.w: Legionnaires' disease is not transmitted person to person, so it cannot be caught from a workmate; infection comes only from inhaling contaminated aerosols.

n.2: The incubation period is around 2 to 10 days, but the real reason is that person-to-person spread does not occur at all.
n.1: Many aerosol sources besides cooling towers can cause infection.
n.0: Exposure to an ill workmate confers no immunity and is not a route of infection.

10.q: Over four months a calorifier's stored temperature records read 62, 61, 60 and 58°C. What does this trend indicate and require?
o: A perfect result needing no attention because none has failed yet
That the thermometer should be thrown away as clearly faulty
A downward drift to investigate before it breaches control
That monitoring should now stop since the figures are close
10.w: Even though the latest figure is still near target, a steady decline signals a developing fault (such as a failing thermostat or scaling) that trend review lets you catch early.

n.0: A downward drift is a warning sign, not a perfect result.
n.1: A consistent fall points to a system issue, not a faulty instrument.
n.3: A concerning trend is a reason to maintain, not stop, monitoring.

10.q: Non-return (check) valves at a TMV are there to do what?
o: Store extra water ready for later periods of low demand
Stop hot and cold water crossing over between the two supplies
Increase the delivered water temperature at the outlet
Filter limescale out of the blended water at the tap
10.w: Check valves prevent crossflow between the hot and cold supplies, which could otherwise upset temperatures or contaminate a supply.

n.0: Check valves do not store water.
n.2: Check valves do not raise the delivery temperature.
n.3: Check valves prevent backflow; they do not filter scale.

10.q: Which combination best describes what a properly completed monitoring record entry should contain?
o: Only the temperature reading itself and a tick to show it was acceptable
The date, the task or outlet, the reading, the result, who did it and any action taken
The outlet reference plus the initials of whoever happened to be on shift during that week
A photograph of the thermometer with the time automatically stamped onto the picture
10.w: A good record is traceable and complete: date, what was checked, the reading obtained, whether it passed or failed, who carried it out and what action followed if it was out of range.

n.0: A bare reading with a tick omits date, location, operative and action.
n.2: An outlet and vague initials with no reading or result cannot evidence control.
n.3: A photo alone is not a structured record and misses result and action.

10.q: After finishing a remedial task and completing a control check, what should the operative do?
o: Record the work and readings and report anything out of range
Only tell a colleague verbally and keep no written record at all
Record only the readings that happened to pass the control check
Leave the site straight away without writing anything down at all
10.w: Accurate records of the work and readings, with any out-of-range findings reported, keep the responsible person informed and the control scheme reliable.

n.1: A verbal word to a colleague is not a reliable record.
n.2: Recording only passing readings hides the failures needing action.
n.3: Leaving no record means faults and work cannot be tracked.

10.q: During flushing you must gently open the outlet to limit aerosol. What should you also consider about your own position and PPE?
o: Your position does not matter as long as the tap is opened slowly
Stand clear of the spray path and use the PPE the risk assessment specifies
PPE is quite unnecessary here, because flushing is not really a cleaning task
Face PPE is only ever needed when flushing hot outlets
10.w: Even with gentle opening, some aerosol is produced, so the operative should keep out of the direct spray path and wear the respiratory and other PPE the site risk assessment specifies for the task.

n.0: Where you stand affects exposure; gentle opening reduces but does not remove aerosol.
n.3: Aerosol from cold outlets can also carry organisms, so PPE is not limited to hot outlets.
n.2: Flushing still generates aerosol, so specified PPE remains relevant.

10.q: What is the minimum return temperature that should be recorded coming back to a calorifier on a circulating hot water system?
o: At least 50°C returning back to the calorifier
Around 60°C, which is the flow and storage figure
Around 45°C, which sits inside the danger zone
Around 55°C, above the minimum the return needs
10.w: The return temperature to the calorifier should be at least 50°C.

n.1: 60°C is the flow and storage figure, not the return minimum.
n.2: 45°C is inside the danger zone and below the required return figure.
n.3: 55°C is higher than the minimum needed for the return leg.

10.q: A building has stood empty during a long refurbishment and water has sat unused in the pipework. What does this change mean for the existing risk assessment?
o: The assessment only needs review once the building is gone
The assessment is automatically cancelled and not replaced
Nothing changes at all because the building is exactly the same shape
The assessment should be reviewed as stagnation changes risk
10.w: A change of use or a period during which the system is left stagnant is exactly the kind of change that can invalidate an assessment, so it must be reviewed and controls applied before normal use resumes.

n.0: Waiting until demolition ignores the risk to people using the reoccupied building.
n.1: An assessment is never simply cancelled; it must be reviewed and kept current.
n.2: The physical shape is irrelevant; the water conditions have changed materially.

10.q: You are carrying out water hygiene checks and notice a stored hot water temperature is far too low. What should you do?
o: Say nothing about it at all so as to avoid causing extra work
Ignore it entirely, because it is simply not on your written task list
Wait several months and just mention it at the next annual review
Record the reading and report it promptly to the responsible person
10.w: The written scheme requires readings to be recorded and problems reported promptly so control can be restored quickly.

n.0: Staying silent leaves a known risk uncontrolled.
n.1: Everyone has a duty to report problems they find, even outside usual tasks.
n.2: A control failure needs prompt action, not delay until the next review.

10.q: Two years after it was written, a site's risk assessment has never been looked at again despite a major re-plumbing of the building. What is the main failing?
o: The assessment was simply written on the wrong grade of paper
The assessment used far too few proper technical words
The assessment should have been thrown away after twelve months
The assessment was not reviewed after a significant alteration that could change the risk
10.w: Significant alterations to the pipework are a clear trigger to review the assessment; leaving it untouched means new dead legs, routes or plant may be uncontrolled and unassessed.

n.1: The vocabulary used is not the compliance failing here.
n.2: Assessments are reviewed and updated, not discarded after a year.
n.0: The medium it is written on is irrelevant to its validity.

10.q: Why is a TMV preferred over simply mixing hot and cold with two separate taps for vulnerable users?
o: Two separate taps are cheaper, so they are always the required choice
Two separate taps control the legionella risk far better than a valve
A TMV needs no cold water supply connected in order to work
It reliably holds a safe temperature and reacts if a supply changes
10.w: A TMV automatically maintains the set blended temperature and fails safe if the cold supply drops, protection two manual taps cannot give.

n.0: Cost does not make two manual taps the safe choice for vulnerable users.
n.1: Neither taps nor a TMV control legionella; temperatures do that.
n.2: A TMV does need a cold supply to blend.

10.q: Which of the following best describes the temperature band that most favours Legionella?
o: Any cold water sitting at a temperature below 10°C
Boiling water held at 100°C straight from the kettle
Near-freezing water held very close to 0°C in unheated cold pipes
Warm water roughly between 20°C and 45°C, around body heat
10.w: Warm water in the 20– 45°C band, peaking near 37°C, most favours growth.

n.2: Near-freezing water keeps the bacteria dormant.
n.1: Boiling water destroys the bacteria.
n.0: Below 10°C the bacteria are cold and dormant.

10.q: Why should debris and dead insects never be left inside a storage tank?
o: They noticeably increase the pressure of the incoming mains supply
They cool the stored water down far below safe levels
They decompose and provide nutrients for bacterial growth
They give the stored water a strong taste of chlorine
10.w: Decomposing debris and insects release nutrients that feed bacteria and support biofilm, so they must be removed by cleaning.

n.0: Material in the tank has no effect on mains pressure.
n.1: Debris does not cool the water.
n.3: Debris does not create a chlorine taste.

10.q: During a survey you find a shower that has not been used for several weeks. Before anyone uses it, the safest action is to:
o: Running a high-pressure electric power shower directly over the body
A spray tap deliberately misting fine water into the air
Slowly filling a bucket from a low tap without any splashing
A cooling tower releasing fine drift across the rooftop
10.w: Flushing clears the stagnant water that may have grown Legionella before anyone creates a spray.

n.0: A power shower produces a fine breathable spray.
n.1: A spray tap deliberately mists water into the air.
n.3: Cooling tower drift is a well-known aerosol source.

10.q: When mixing a disinfectant to the required strength, what should the operative follow?
o: Simply double the stated amount just to be on the safe side
The dosing instructions in the method statement and on the product
Whatever a passing member of the public happens to suggest at the time
Their own rough judgement of roughly about the right amount
10.w: The correct concentration comes from the method statement and product instructions, not guesswork, so that disinfection is effective and safe.

n.0: Overdosing wastes chemical, raises hazards and is not the specified strength.
n.2: An unqualified passer-by is not a reliable source for a safety-critical dose.
n.3: An approximate dose may be too weak to work or too strong to handle safely.

10.q: While cleaning a shower head you notice it is furred with scale and slime. What should you do?
o: Descale and disinfect it fully, wearing PPE, and record what you found
Give it a brief rinse under the tap and then refit it just as before
Refit it exactly as it is, since it does still spray water
Bin it and simply leave the shower running with no head at all
10.w: Scale and slime hold legionella, so the head is properly descaled and disinfected with PPE worn, and the finding is recorded.

n.1: A quick rinse leaves the scale and biofilm that harbour legionella in place.
n.2: Refitting a fouled head keeps a contaminated aerosol source in service.
n.3: Leaving no head is not a controlled repair and the finding still needs recording.

10.q: A written scheme for controlling the risk has been prepared for a site. What is your duty as an operative in relation to it?
o: Rewrite the control scheme yourself to suit your own preferred way of working
Carry out your tasks as the scheme sets out and record what you do
Ignore it, since the scheme is only advisory guidance
Keep it locked away and unread to keep it in good condition
10.w: Operatives must follow the written scheme, complete their tasks correctly and keep records as required.

n.0: Altering the control scheme is the responsible person's role, not an operative's.
n.2: The scheme is a legal control measure that must be followed, not ignored.
n.3: The scheme must be used and understood, not hidden away.

10.q: Why should a little-used outlet be opened gently and slowly when you flush it?
o: Because the tap itself could break if it were opened too quickly
To reduce the spray and aerosol released into the air
To save a useful amount of water while flushing it
To stop the pipework from making a loud banging noise
10.w: Opening gently limits the fine aerosol created, reducing the breathable spray that could carry legionella.

n.0: Preventing damage is not the health reason for opening gently.
n.2: Saving water is not the reason; controlling aerosol is.
n.3: Noise is not the concern; releasing less breathable spray is.

10.q: A site manager proposes lowering the calorifier storage temperature from 60°C to 52°C to cut energy bills and reduce scald risk. Under ACOP L8, is this acceptable?
o: Yes, provided that all the outlets still manage to reach 45°C
Yes, if a chemical dosing system is added to the system at the same time
No; storage must stay at 60°C, and scalding is controlled with TMVs
Yes, because 52°C is warm enough to prevent any bacterial growth
10.w: Storage must be kept at 60°C or above for legionella control; it must never be reduced to save energy or manage scalding. Scald risk is controlled at the point of use with thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs), not by lowering stored temperature.

n.0: Reducing storage to 52°C breaches the control standard regardless of outlet temperature.
n.1: Chemical dosing does not permit abandoning the 60°C storage standard.
n.3: 52°C is within the range where legionella can survive in storage and is not safe.

10.q: Which practice helps keep the base of a calorifier free from harmful sediment?
o: Never opening the vessel once it is installed
Regular draining and inspection of the base
Keeping the drain valve permanently sealed
Lowering the storage temperature below 50°C
10.w: Regular draining and inspection of the base removes sediment before it can shelter bacteria.

n.0: Never opening the vessel lets sludge build up unchecked.
n.2: A permanently sealed drain prevents the base being cleared of sludge.
n.3: Lowering the temperature encourages bacterial growth rather than controlling it.

10.q: Which factor about the aerosol itself most influences whether inhaling it could cause Legionnaires' disease?
o: Whether the droplets are fine enough to be breathed deep into the lungs
Whether the spray simply looks coloured or clear
Whether droplets are large enough to be seen falling
Whether the water tastes unpleasant when swallowed
10.w: It is the fine, respirable droplets that can be carried deep into the lungs; these are the ones that matter for causing infection when they contain Legionella.

n.2: Large droplets that quickly fall are less likely to be inhaled deeply into the lungs.
n.3: Taste relates to swallowing, which is not the route of infection.
n.1: The colour or clarity of the spray does not determine infectivity.

10.q: Why are the nearest and furthest outlets on a loop chosen as sentinel points?
o: They represent the range of temperatures across the system
They are the only outlets that anyone ever actually uses
They are simply the taps closest to the staff car park
They are always among the cheapest taps to install
10.w: The nearest and furthest outlets show the extremes of the system, so monitoring them reflects overall performance.

n.1: Sentinels are chosen for their position on the loop, not usage popularity.
n.2: Distance from the car park is irrelevant to sentinel selection.
n.3: Cost of installation is not why sentinel points are chosen.

10.q: Why should cold water pipes be insulated (lagged)?
o: Only to stop the pipe from looking untidy on the wall
To help keep the water below 20°C by shielding it
To make the water flow through the pipe much faster
To raise the water temperature above 20°C deliberately
10.w: Insulating cold pipes shields them from surrounding heat so the water stays below 20 degrees C.

n.0: Appearance is not the reason; temperature control is.
n.2: Insulation does not change the flow rate.
n.3: The aim is to keep cold water cool, not to warm it up.
